analysis.investment_thesis: Exim Routes fails nearly every quantitative filter I require: P/B of ~9.9x, P/E of 37.5, only two years of positive earnings, and zero years of positive operating cash flow in five years. The stock trades at roughly 3.7x its Graham Number (~INR 39), offering no margin of safety whatsoever.
key_strengths: Revenue grew rapidly from INR 4 Cr (2021) to INR 121 Cr (2025), demonstrating operational scaling
Debt-to-Equity of 0.36 (Borrowings INR 9 Cr vs Equity INR 25 Cr) is the one metric that passes my filter
ROCE of 55% and ROE of 54% are superficially impressive, though unconfirmed by cash flows
key_risks: Cash flow destruction: OCF negative every single year (0/5 positive); FCF was -INR 9 Cr in 2025 despite INR 8 Cr reported net profit — earnings quality is deeply suspect
Minimal earnings track record: Net profit was zero for 2021, 2022, and 2023 — only two years of profitability; Graham requires at minimum 3-5 consecutive profitable years
Extreme overvaluation: P/B ~9.9x (Graham ceiling is 1.5x) and price of INR 146 vs Graham Number of ~INR 39 means you are paying nearly 4x fair value for unproven earning power
red_flags: OCF negative all 5 years — profits are not being converted to cash, suggesting aggressive revenue recognition or severe working capital drag
Incorporated April 2019 — only a 6-year-old company with a mere 2-year profit history; no durability established
No dividend history whatsoever; shareholders receive nothing while management consumes capital
Market cap of INR 248 Cr vs Total Equity of INR 25 Cr implies the market is pricing in decades of growth that may never materialise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By every quantitative standard I have applied for over fifty years, Exim Routes is a speculation dressed as an investment. The Graham Number — computed as √(22.5 × ~INR 4.7 EPS × ~INR 14.7 BVPS) — yields approximately INR 39, against a market price of INR 146. That is a 275% premium to intrinsic value, the precise opposite of my required margin of safety. P/E at 37.5 is nearly 2.5× my maximum threshold of 15, and the Price-to-Book of roughly 9.9× makes this company appear priced for perfection in a commodity recycled-paper business where no durable competitive advantage is evident.

What troubles me most is the disconnect between reported profits and cash reality. The company shows INR 8 Cr net profit in FY2025 yet generated negative INR 5 Cr from operations and negative INR 9 Cr free cash flow. In my experience, when a company cannot convert reported earnings into cash, one must question whether those earnings are real. The business is funded almost entirely by external financing (Financing CF +INR 11 Cr in 2025) rather than its own operations — a pattern I associate with capital consumption, not wealth creation. Mr. Market may be excited by 134% revenue CAGR, but I will not pay for a story; I insist on demonstrated, cash-backed earning power. This company has neither the history nor the price to merit a disciplined investor's capital.
